paper_title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: An agents capabilities depend jointly on its brainthe language model that reasons and selects actionsand its bodythe harness that defines its tool interfaces, action space, memory, and execution workflow (Lou et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026c). Accordingly, progress has followed two complementary directions. Model training improves the agents learned policy through supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and self-distillation (Xia et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b). Harness optimization improves the surrounding system with the model fixed, through iterative modification of prompts, tools, and control flow guided by execution feedback (Lou et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026), or population-based evolution that generates, evaluates, and recombines competing harness designs (Lee et al., 2026c; Zhang et al., 2026h). These directions meet in model harness co-evolution, where model training and harness optimization jointly adapt an agent to its task domain (Chen et al., 2026c; Luo et al., 2026a). Recent systems demonstrate the promise of this approach across tool use, mathematical reasoning, search-based question answering, and chess (Chen et al., 2026b,d; Kim et al., 2026). co-evolution round couples harness evolution with model adaptation. Starting from modelharness pair (H𝑡, 𝜃𝑡), execution feedback F𝑡 guides changes to the harness, whose requirements in turn shape the models next adaptation (Chen et al., 2026d). As either component evolves, the harnesss execution requirements and the models learned capabilities can drift apart. In this setting, we first identify and formalize the brainbody mismatch problem: Problem Definition During modelharness co-evolution, pair (H𝑡, 𝜃𝑡) exhibits brainbody mismatch when the behaviors required by H𝑡 diverge from those learned by 𝜃𝑡, or when H𝑡 restricts the use of capabilities already present in 𝜃𝑡. The problem is to maintain their compatibility through successive rounds of harness-model co-adaptation. In plain terms, the model may struggle to operate its harness, and the harness may underuse its models abilities (Figure 2). Consider two concrete examples. ❶ Interface mismatch. The model emits XML tool calls, while the evolved harness expects JSON, causing otherwise correct calls to be rejected. ❷ Capability mismatch. The harness introduces an active context management tool for deciding what information to retain, summarize, or discard. model unfamiliar with these operations may use it poorly; historical checkpoint 𝜃𝑖 already possesses the relevant capabilities and provides suitable starting point for adaptation. On the harness side, historical design 𝑗 can supply an execution workflow suited to the models capabilities. These examples motivate selecting predecessors whose inherited behaviors and structures support further evolution. Figure 2: Brainbody alignment in modelharness co-evolution. Left: Historical harnesses and checkpoints are recombined and adapted to resolve interface mismatch. Right: Step accuracy versus Turn-level Interface Mismatch Rate (TIMR; 3.1) for ten evolved versions per method, from three-round run evaluated on the Who&When test benchmark. To address this challenge, we propose CoEvo-RSI, framework for modelharness co-evolution through bidirectional historical inheritance. Its evolutionary archive A<𝑡 records earlier harnesses, 2 model checkpoints, their development histories, and execution outcomes. Each round begins with feedback from the current pair. Curator organizes this evidence, and harness editors browse the archive, choose their own historical starting designs, and develop offspring harnesses. For each offspring, the framework selects or merges historical checkpoints to form candidate modelharness pairs. Evaluation identifies promising pair for model adaptation under its harness, and validation determines which pair advances to the next round. The resulting designs, checkpoints, and outcomes extend the archive. This agent-driven inheritance connects the two sides of evolution: harness design draws on accumulated structural experience, while model initialization draws on capabilities suited to the emerging harness. Their coordination makes brainbody alignment the organizing principle of the evolutionary process. Our contributions are: Problem Formalization. We formalize brainbody mismatch in modelharness co-evolution and introduce the turn-level interface mismatch rate (TIMR) as an inexpensive diagnostic signal for observable interface violations. Method Design. We propose CoEvo-RSI, which combines an evolutionary archive with bidirectional historical inheritance. Harness editors select historical starting designs, and model inheritance selects or merges checkpoints to support adaptation under the evolved harness. Empirical Evaluation. We evaluate CoEvo-RSI across multi-agent failure attribution, home care, and SQL tasks, with co-evolved Qwen3.5-9B outperforming Qwen3.8-Max on Who&When Pro (+4.40 agent acc.) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent acc.).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Self-evolving agents improve through changes to external execution systems, learned model parameters, or both (Gao et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). We organize the literature around these optimization targets and the reuse of historical components that connects them. Recursive Harness Improvement. Early agent systems established how external organization can improve models behavior: ReAct interleaves reasoning and actions, Reflexion retains verbal feedback across trials, and Voyager accumulates reusable executable skills (Yao et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023). Agentcomputer interface design further shows how the operations exposed to model shape its effectiveness (Yang et al., 2024). Subsequent work turns these hand-designed mechanisms into optimization targets, evolving context (Zhang et al., 2026g), memory (Zhang et al., 2025a, 2026e; Pan et al., 2026b), planning (Liu et al., 2026b), and retrieval (Lee et al., 2026b). At the system level, harness search jointly modifies prompts, tools, and control flow (Lee et al., 2026a,c; Lin et al., 2026; Lou et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026d,f). AutoHarness synthesizes executable support from environmental feedback, while Meta-Harness gives its proposer access to earlier source code, scores, and execution traces (Lou et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026c). Such access preserves evidence that single scalar score or compressed reflection can omit. Online adaptation extends this process to deployment streams and test-time feedback (Liu et al., 2026c; Nie et al., 2026b; Pan et al., 2026a); population search and reusable repositories retain alternative designs for subsequent exploration (Zhang et al., 2026h; Nie et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026b). The Darwin Gödel Machine similarly grows an archive of self-modifying agents, allowing earlier branches to become stepping stones for later improvements (Zhang et al., 2025c). Together, these approaches expand the search target from isolated modules to complete execution systems. They also motivate preserving design diversity and execution history, which CoEvo-RSI connects to corresponding archive of model checkpoints. Recursive Model Improvement. Model self-improvement converts generated experience into persistent changes in the policy. Three learning loops are particularly relevant. (i) Curricula adapt the source and difficulty of training problems to the learner, including self-play, tool-oriented task genera3 tion, and search-agent training without externally supplied demonstrations (Zhao et al., 2025; Acikgoz et al., 2026; Sundaram et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a,b; Yue et al., 2026). The resulting feedback loop changes which experiences the model encounters as its competence develops. (ii) Supervision turns demonstrations, privileged feedback, or the models own improved behavior into self-distillation targets (Zhao et al., 2026a; Shenfeld et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Lu et al., 2026b). On-policy variants address the learners current behavior, making the distribution of generated trajectories central to what can be learned. (iii) Experience reuse extracts reusable skills and transfers their guidance into model behavior (Xia et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Lu et al., 2026c; Wu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026c). For example, SkillRL jointly evolves hierarchical skill library and the agent policy, linking experience abstraction with subsequent reinforcement learning (Xia et al., 2026). These mechanisms improve the agents intrinsic capabilities, while the harness determines which tools, observations, and execution constraints appear in its training trajectories. This dependence motivates choosing model initialization and adaptation in relation to the harness that will actually execute the policy. ModelHarness Co-Evolution. Joint adaptation closes the loop between the environment presented to policy and the behavior learned under that environment. One line couples (i) context and weights through prompt optimization, continual adaptation, and the transfer of contextual guidance into parameters (Lu et al., 2026a; Tiwari et al., 2026; Tu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026b). second line couples (ii) executable harnesses and policies, extending adaptation to the tools, memory, middleware, and control flow used during rollout (Chen et al., 2026b,c,d; Kim et al., 2026; Qi et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Hebbar et al., 2026; Karten et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2026; TaoLive AIGC LLM Team et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026b). HarnessForge combines fault-guided harness tailoring with harness-conditioned policy alignment (Chen et al., 2026b). Co-Harness alternates validated harness patches with fine-tuning on trajectories generated by the improved scaffold (Chen et al., 2026d), while WHALE alternates rejection-sampling fine-tuning with executable harness search (Kim et al., 2026). third line brings (iii) execution and editing into shared learning process, allowing policies to participate in the evolution of their own support (Luo et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026). These methods establish the value of adapting both sides and expose common dependency: harness update changes the execution requirements, and model update changes which harnesses are effective. CoEvo-RSI makes bidirectional historical inheritance an explicit decision within this loop. Harness editors choose historical starting designs, and model inheritance independently selects or merges archived checkpoints for the resulting requirements. This enables recovery of useful earlier capabilities without tying model initialization to the latest generation or the harnesss parent branch. compares the inheritance procedures of representative frameworks.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: CoEvo-RSI (Figure 3) realizes modelharness co-evolution through bidirectional historical inheritance. An autonomous meta-agent coordinates two complementary decisions: harness editors select and develop historical designs, and model inheritance selects or merges checkpoints for the resulting execution requirements. Evaluation, model adaptation, and promotion turn these inherited components into the next agent, whose outcomes enrich the evolutionary archive.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Evaluation benchmarks. To test whether co-evolution generalizes beyond single harness design, we evaluate CoEvo-RSI on three domains that demand different harness capabilities: long-trajectory reasoning, policy-constrained tool use, and structured device control. ❶ Failure attribution identifies the responsible agent (Who) and the decisive error step (When) in multi-agent trajectories. We hold out 200 TracerTraj (Zhang et al., 2025b) instances for validation during evolution, leaving 3,400 single-error training instances drawn from the remaining TracerTraj data, CORRECT-Error (Yu et al., 2026a), AFTraj (Zhang et al., 2026a), and self-constructed trajectories. The Hand and Algo. subsets of Who&When (Zhang et al., 2025d), Who&When Pro (Liu et al., 2026a), and TraceElephant (Chen et al., 2026a) are reserved for out-of-distribution (OOD) testing. ❷ Role-aware text-to-SQL requires generating SQL only when the users role authorizes every referenced table and column, and refusing otherwise. We use the Spider subset of the RBAC benchmark (Fei et al., 2026) with its official split and its BIRD subset as an OOD test without any training. ❸ Smart-home instruction following maps instructions to device operations and rejects infeasible ones. We use the valid (VM) and invalid (IM) multi-device subsets of HomeBench (Li et al., 2025) with official splits. Scope: affordable domain specialization We deliberately choose specialized benchmarks because CoEvo-RSI targets compact agents for vertical applications. Examples include lightweight failure-attribution evaluators for large-scale RL training, local smart-home controllers, and enterprise website assistants operating under strict database-access permissions. Each run has ten rounds with K=8 harness candidates per round. The selected Qwen3.5-9B checkpoint samples up to three trajectories per training task under its paired harness at temperature 1, stopping at the first verifier-accepted one. The accepted trajectories are used for one epoch of full-parameter SFT (learning rate 5e-6, batch size 8) on four H100 GPUs. Full data, hyperparameter, baseline, and prompt details are in Sections and E.

sections.title: 4.3 Ablation Study
sections.content: We compare full CoEvo-RSI with three variants over ten rounds on Who&When Algo. (Figure 4): Harness-only evolves the harness with frozen model; Model-only trains under the initial harness; and Latest-only co-evolves both using only the latest generation. ❶ Joint evolution. Harness-only has lower SA than full CoEvo-RSI in every round and TIMR above 1% in eight of ten rounds, versus at most 0.22% for full CoEvo-RSI. Model-only maintains near-zero TIMR with SA at most 35%, indicating that interface compatibility alone is insufficient for task success. ❷ Historical reuse. Latest-only regresses at round 4 and finishes with the lowest SA. Full CoEvo-RSI recovers from its round-4 dip, reusing round-4 weights with new harnesses at rounds 6 and 8 to reach 61.11% and 61.90% AA. Together, these results support complementary roles for bidirectional inheritance and historical reuse in task performance, interface compatibility, and recovery.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented CoEvo-RSI, bi-level framework that addresses the brainbody mismatch problem in modelharness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback guide harness development from historical designs, model checkpoint selection or merging, and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness. Using only SFT on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes compact task model competitive with larger models across multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. Together, these findings highlight brainbody alignment as central consideration for self-improving agents and bidirectional historical inheritance as practical route to evolving execution scaffolds (body) and intrinsic capabilities (brain) together.

sections.title: A Experimental Details
sections.content: This section details the benchmarks, data, initial harnesses, and hyperparameters behind 4.1. In every domain, training, validation, and test sets are disjoint at the level of sample IDs, tasks, and trajectories. The same validation set guides harness and checkpoint selection and promotion during evolution; test sets are reserved for performance reporting. For failure attribution, all 200 validation instances are held out from TracerTraj and removed from the training pool (A.2). A.1 Common Setup Evolution. All domains run ten rounds of co-evolution with K=8 harness candidates per round. The candidate-sensitivity study in 4.4 is the exception and uses three rounds. The meta-agent is DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with high reasoning effort, running inside Codex. In each round, the meta-agent receives validation rollouts of the incumbent modelharness pair. Each editor browses the historical archive, selects an inheritance base, and develops copy of that harness using the execution evidence and reusable historical designs. The prompt it receives is listed in E. Each candidate is then evaluated on the full validation set. Candidates are compared using the domain-specific objectives in Table 4. Task model and rollout. The task model is Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) with thinking enabled at high reasoning effort. It is served with vLLM and sampled with temperature 1.0, top-𝑝 0.95, and top-𝑘 20. Per-domain generation budgets, context lengths, and turn limits appear in Table 4. Model training. For each training task, the selected model 𝜃𝑡 samples up to three trajectories under its paired harness H𝑡, stopping at the first verifier-accepted one. These accepted trajectories, together with selected high-quality accepted trajectories replayed from earlier rounds, are used for one epoch of full-parameter SFT of the same model with ms-swift (Zhao et al., 2024). Training uses AdamW with learning rate 5 106, cosine schedule with 3% warmup, per-device batch size of 1, and 4 gradient-accumulation steps. It runs on four H100 GPUs with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, bf16, and gradient checkpointing. The global batch size is 8 in all domains, and long-context domains additionally use sequence parallelism of size 2. A.2 Failure Attribution Task. Given the full log of failed multi-agent run, the system must name the agent responsible for the failure (Who) and the decisive step at which the failure becomes unrecoverable (When). Benchmarks. Table 5 lists all splits; all four test benchmarks are held out from training and evolutionary selection. Who&When Pro (Liu et al., 2026a) is evaluated on its 1,750 multi-agent, text-only trajectories; we exclude single-agent trajectories, on which attribution is nearly saturated. For TraceElephant (Chen et al., 2026a), we drop records whose decisive-step annotation is missing or invalid, which leaves 219 evaluable instances. Training and validation data. Training instances come from TracerTraj (Zhang et al., 2025b), CORRECT-Error (Yu et al., 2026a), AFTraj (Zhang et al., 2026a), and small set of trajectories we construct ourselves. We keep only trajectories that contain single error, use dense one-based step indices, and have responsible agent consistent with the decisive step. Of the 1,818 filtered TracerTraj instances, 200 are held out for validation and the remaining 1,618 are retained for training. Together with 1,230 CORRECT-Error, 430 AFTraj, and 122 self-constructed instances, this gives 3,400 training instances. The 200-instance TracerTraj validation set guides candidate and checkpoint selection and promotion. The source studies explicitly document evaluation-data isolation in their respective protocols (Zhang et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026a). We further rigorously checked our training data against the held-out TracerTraj validation set, Who&When Hand, Who&When Algo., Who&When Pro, and TraceElephant. These checks confirmed separation at the sample-ID and task levels and found no identical or highly similar trajectories across training and evaluation. Metrics. Agent accuracy (AA, reported as Who) is the fraction of instances whose predicted responsible agent matches the annotation. Step accuracy (SA, reported as When) is the fraction whose predicted decisive step matches the annotated step exactly. The harness requires the model to answer through structured final_answer tool, so predictions are parsed and scored by exact match against the ground truth without an LLM judge. Results are reported separately for each subset. Initial harness. The hand-written harness exposes the trajectory summary-first: the model initially sees only per-step metadata such as step IDs and agent names. It must call inspect to read the full content of step, and it submits the agent and step through final_answer. Ground-truth labels are never exposed, and the episode is limited to 20 turns. A.3 Role-Aware Text-to-SQL Task. Each instance pairs natural-language question over database with user role whose columnand operation-level access policy is given. request is authorized only if every table, column, and operation it needs is covered by the roles policy (Fei et al., 2026). We run Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026c) and Self-Harness (Zhang et al., 2026d) from their official implementations and add failure attribution domain adapter for each. Both start from the same task model (Qwen3.5-9B), the same hand-written initial harness, and the same 200 held-out TracerTraj validation instances as CoEvo-RSI. Each runs for ten rounds. Both baselines use the same meta-agent LLM and settings as CoEvo-RSI, namely DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with high reasoning effort, and each keeps its officially recommended proposer workflow. sections.title: B Scope and Interpretation of TIMR
sections.content: Diagnostic scope. TIMR (Equation (5)) measures the frequency of observable interface violations within modelharness pair: calls to unavailable tools, interface-contract violations, and malformed outputs. These events expose concrete aspect of brainbody mismatch at the execution boundary and can be checked directly from traces. Their low verification cost makes TIMR useful for diagnosing candidate pairs during evolution. The broader problem definition also covers learned capabilities that harness underuses or constrains. Such cases can produce valid tool calls throughout an unsuccessful 24 Table 9: Hyperparameters of the RL baselines. TIMR therefore provides focused operational view of interface compatibility within this broader evaluation. Raw TIMR lies in [0, 1] (0100%); Figure 8 uses global minmax scaling across all harnesscheckpoint pairs to [0, 1]. Relationship to task performance. Task success depends jointly on interface use, reasoning, access to relevant evidence, and the execution workflow. The ablations in Figure 4 illustrate these distinct factors: Model-only maintains near-zero TIMR with step accuracy at most 35%, whereas Harnessonly has TIMR above 1% in eight of ten rounds and lower step accuracy than full CoEvo-RSI in every round. Full CoEvo-RSI keeps TIMR at or below 0.22% while improving task performance. These observations support using TIMR together with task scores to distinguish execution friction from other performance bottlenecks. They provide diagnostic evidence; attributing performance gain specifically to lower TIMR would require controlled interventions that isolate interface behavior from changes in reasoning, information access, and execution budget. Role in co-evolution. CoEvo-RSI reads TIMR alongside task performance when proposing checkpoint selections or merges, and uses validation task scores to select and promote modelharness pairs (Equations (12) and (13)). low TIMR identifies pair whose observed interactions largely satisfy the harnesss interface requirements; task evaluation establishes how effectively that pair solves the intended problems. This division gives TIMR practical role as an inexpensive diagnostic signal, with the value of an evolutionary update assessed through downstream performance.

sections.title: C Interpreting Comparisons with Frontier Models
sections.content: Our evaluation asks how far co-evolution can bring compact task model toward frontier-level performance in given domain. The compared models start from markedly different capability levels: on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, Qwen3.5-9B (Reasoning) scores 11, compared with 36 for DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 (Max) and 45 for GLM-5.3 (Max) (Artificial Analysis, 2026a,b,c). These independent measurements contextualize the capability gap behind our task comparisons. Against this background, approaching or matching frontier systems on several demanding tasks is substantive outcome for 9B model. For example, CoEvo-RSI achieves 95.51% Spider AC-F1 against 95.85% for the strongest system on this metric, Pi + MiniMax-M3  (Table 2)  , and 75.51% HomeBench VM success against 75.10% for DeepSeek-V4-Pro  (Table 3)  . Such proximity remains meaningful when individual metric rankings vary across benchmarks. 25 All SFT supervision comes from Qwen3.5-9Bs own verifier-accepted trajectories, generated by the selected checkpoint or, through replay, by earlier checkpoints and retained through rejection sampling (A.1). The meta-agent guides harness evolution and checkpoint inheritance; model training consolidates the 9B task models successful execution experience. We view the resulting competitiveness as evidence of how much useful capability can be elicited and consolidated from compact model through coordinated modelharness evolution. Positioning: affordable domain specialization. As frontier models advance, complementary deployment need is to make compact models effective within well-defined domain. We position CoEvo-RSI as tool for this need, particularly for frequent agent calls where cost and responsetime budgets shape system design. Potential applications include device manufacturers integrating smart-home control and RL systems requiring failure-attribution feedback on repeated agent rollouts. These needs motivate our three benchmark domains: smart-home instruction following for device execution, multi-agent failure attribution for automated diagnosis, and role-aware text-to-SQL for policy-constrained data access. Each tests task-specific behavior under concrete operational requirements. The results support this practical motivation: CoEvo-RSI achieves 68.39% agent accuracy on Who&When Hand versus 60.34% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Under the API pricing in Figure 7, their full evaluation passes over Hand and Algo. cost $0.16 and $3.55, respectively, approximately 22 lower for CoEvo-RSI. Together with the close Spider and HomeBench results above, this demonstrates the value of specialization for delivering competitive task performance at low recurring cost. Small differences on individual metrics can be acceptable when the resulting agent meets an applications quality requirements and operating budget. Our aim is to give practitioners an affordable modelharness pair optimized for the tasks they repeatedly need to solve.

sections.title: D Comparison with Related Evolution Frameworks
sections.content: Table 10 compares six modelharness co-evolution methods and two harness-only methods through the sources of their inherited structure and capabilities. Harness history supports several forms of reuse, including archive-guided refinement, search over previous programs, and persistent component updates. On the model side, the compared co-evolution procedures continue the current checkpoint or inherit the policy associated with parent branch. CoEvo-RSI makes both sources explicit decisions over the evolutionary archive: harness editors choose historical starting designs, and model inheritance independently selects or merges historical checkpoints for the resulting harnesses. This flexibility allows structure and capabilities from different generations to form new candidate pairs, whose execution feedback guides selection and subsequent adaptation. Bidirectional historical inheritance expands the candidate space for further co-evolution. Meta-Agent Prompts The prompt given to the meta-agent in each round has two parts. The first is shared skeleton that is identical across domains (Prompt A) and fixes the evidence discipline, workflow, and permission boundary.
